title: حِكَايَةُ صَاحِبِ الْجَزَائِرِ السُّودِ
titleEn: The Tale of the Lord of the Black Isles
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 41–48 (continuing directly from nights-06, whose text ends with the maiden's verse-challenge to the four colored fish and their first burning to charcoal before the astonished vizier), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project’s own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition’s own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition’s — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor’s slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 7 opens with the vizier reporting the scene from Night 6 to the Sultan, who insists on seeing it with his own eyes: a second catch of the four-colored fish is fried, and this time a huge black slave — not the jewelled maiden — rises from a crack in the kitchen wall, chants the same verse-challenge to the fish, and the fish likewise burn. Astonished, the Sultan interrogates the fisherman, learns of a remote pool ringed by four mountains, and marches his whole army there — only to dismiss them all and go on alone, by night and in disguise, when no one can say they have ever seen the pool before. Days of solitary travel bring him to a deserted, richly furnished black-stone castle; there he finds a beautiful young man, richly dressed but grief-stricken, who turns out to be a man turned half to stone — his lower body marble, his upper body still living flesh. The young man tells his own story: king of this city and its four mountains after his father Mahmoud, “Lord of the Black Isles,” he was married to a cousin who loved him intensely, until he overheard his own slave-girls reveal that she drugged his nightly drink and slipped away each night to a squalid hut, where she lay with a repulsive, ailing black slave. Testing this himself, the young man feigns drinking the drugged cup, follows his wife in secret through the city — whose gates open to her at a word — to the hut, and witnesses the slave’s coarse rebuke of her lateness and her abject pleading — and, unable to bear it, comes down, takes his own sword, and strikes the slave first, believing him dead, exactly as dawn cuts Shahrazad off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language toward Classical Arabic here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about infidelity, coarse insult, and violence, and is translated that way.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīd
sentences.l: So when it was the seventh night, she said, "It has reached me, O fortunate king,
sentences.i: Now when the seventh night came, she said, "It has reached me, O fortunate King,

sentences.t: أَنَّهُ لَمَّا تَكَلَّمَ السَّمَكُ وَقَلَبَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الطَّاجِنَ بِالْقَضِيبِ وَخَرَجَتْ مِنْ مَوْضِعِ مَا جَاءَتْ وَالْتَأَمَ الْحَائِطُ
sentences.tr: annahu lammā takallama al-samaku wa-qalabati al-ṣabiyyatu al-ṭājina bi-al-qaḍībi wa-kharajat min mawḍiʿi mā jāʾat wa-iltaʾama al-ḥāʾiṭu
sentences.l: that when the fish spoke, and the maiden turned the pan over with the rod, and went out from the place from which she had come, and the wall closed up —
sentences.i: that when the fish spoke, and the maiden overturned the pan with the rod and went out the way she had come, and the wall closed up again —
sentences.n: This opens mid-scene, recapping the very end of Night 6: the maiden's verse-challenge to the frying fish and her withdrawal back into the wall.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قَامَ الْوَزِيرُ وَقَالَ هَذَا أَمْرٌ لَا يَجِبُ إِخْفَاؤُهُ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāma al-wazīru wa-qāla hādhā amrun lā yajibu ikhfāʾuhu ʿalā al-maliki
sentences.l: at that, the vizier rose and said, "This is a matter — its concealment from the king is not proper."
sentences.i: at that, the vizier rose and said, "This is a matter that ought not to be hidden from the king."

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ وَأَخْبَرَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu taqaddama ilā al-maliki wa-akhbarahu
sentences.l: Then indeed he came forward to the king and informed him
sentences.i: Then he went before the king and told him
sentences.n: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ, 'then indeed he', is the recurring narrative connective of this prose — read simply as 'then'.

sentences.t: بِالْقِصَّةِ وَبِمَا شَاهَدَهُ قُدَّامَهُ فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ لَا بُدَّ إِنِّي أَنْظُرَ بِعَيْنِي
sentences.tr: bi-al-qiṣṣati wa-bimā shāhadahu quddāmahu fa-qāla al-maliku lā budda innī anẓura bi-ʿaynī
sentences.l: of the story, and of what he had witnessed before him. Then the king said, "There is no escape — I must look with my own eye."
sentences.i: of the story, and of what he had witnessed with his own eyes. The king said, "I must see this for myself."
sentences.n: لَا بُدَّ إِنِّي أَنْظُرَ, 'there is no escape, [that] I look', follows لَا بُدَّ directly with إِنَّ + subjunctive rather than the Classical لَا بُدَّ أَنْ or لَا بُدَّ لِي مِنْ — a Middle Arabic looseness of government kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَأَرْسَلَ خَلْفَ الصَّيَّادِ وَ أَمَرَهُ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ بِأَرْبَعِ سَمَكَاتٍ مِثْلَ الْأَوَّلِ، ثُمَّ رَسَمَ عَلَيْهِ،
sentences.tr: fa-arsala khalfa al-ṣayyādi wa-amarahu an yaʾtiya bi-arbaʿi samakātin mithla al-awwali, thumma rasama ʿalayhi,
sentences.l: So he sent after the fisherman and ordered him to bring four fish like the first, then he laid a decree upon him —
sentences.i: So he sent for the fisherman and commanded him to bring four fish like the first; then he laid a strict charge upon him —
sentences.n: رَسَمَ عَلَيْهِ, 'he issued a decree upon him', uses رَسَمَ in its technical sense of a royal command, not 'to draw'. The commas after الْأَوَّلِ and عَلَيْهِ are printed in the edition itself and are kept as its own punctuation, not added here.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الصَّيَّادَ نَزَلَ وَأُذِنَ لَهُ بِالسَّمَكِ فِي الْحَالِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ṣayyāda nazala wa-udhina lahu bi-al-samaki fī al-ḥāli
sentences.l: — then indeed the fisherman went down, and leave was granted him for the fish at once.
sentences.i: — so the fisherman went down, and was at once given leave to fish.
sentences.n: وَأُذِنَ لَهُ, an impersonal passive with no agent named, likely recalls the efrit's rule from Night 6 that the pool may be fished only once a day — the fisherman is simply found to be within his rights to fish again.

sentences.t: فَأَمْضَي الْمَلِكُ أَنْ يُعْطُوهُ أَرْبَعَمِائَةَ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-amḍā al-maliku an yuʿṭūhu arbaʿamiʾata dīnārin
sentences.l: Then the king ordered that they give him four hundred dinars.
sentences.i: Then the king gave orders that he be given four hundred dinars.
sentences.n: أَمْضَى here carries its technical sense 'to ratify, carry into effect' (an order), not 'to sign' in the narrow modern sense. The edition spells its final long vowel with plain ي rather than the expected ى (alif maqṣūra); kept as printed and read amḍā.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى الْوَزِيرِ وَقَالَ لَهُ، قُمْ أَنْتَ وَاقْلِ السَّمَكَ هُمَا قُدَّامِي
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata al-maliku ilā al-wazīri wa-qāla lahu, qum anta wa-iqli al-samaka humā quddāmī
sentences.l: Then the king turned to the vizier and said to him, "Rise, you, and fry the fish — the two of them — before me."
sentences.i: Then the king turned to the vizier and said to him, "Get up, you, and fry the fish here before me."
sentences.n: هُمَا, 'the two of them' (dual), does not agree with السَّمَك (a mass noun, not dual) and sits oddly in the sentence; it may be a misprint for هُنَا, 'here', but is kept exactly as the archive prints it, per the pilot's practice with similarly obscure forms.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: So the vizier said, "hearing and obedience."
sentences.i: The vizier answered, "With hearing and obedience."

sentences.t: السَّمَكَ وَرَكَّبَ الطَّاجِنَ عَلَى النَّارِ وَرَمَى فِيهِ السَّمَكَ
sentences.tr: al-samaka wa-rakkaba al-ṭājina ʿalā al-nāri wa-ramā fīhi al-samaka
sentences.l: — the fish: and he set the pan upon the fire and threw the fish into it.
sentences.i: — and so, taking the fish, he set the pan on the fire and threw the fish into it.
sentences.n: السَّمَكَ opens this clause as a fronted, accusative object with no verb of its own expressed (perhaps an elided أَخَذَ, 'he took'); read here as a topic picked up by the following clause. رَكَّبَ is used in its colloquial sense 'to set up, put in place' rather than its Classical 'to mount, ride'.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْحَائِطِ قَدِ انْشَقَّ وَخَرَجَ مِنْهُ عَبْدٌ أَسْوَدُ كَأَنَّهُ طَوْدٌ مِنَ الْأَطْوَادِ أَوْ مِنْ بَقِيَّةِ قَوْمِ عَادٍ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-ḥāʾiṭi qadi inshaqqa wa-kharaja minhu ʿabdun aswadu kaʾannahu ṭawdun mina al-aṭwādi aw min baqiyyati qawmi ʿādin
sentences.l: And behold, the wall had split open, and there came out of it a black slave, as if he were a mountain-mass among the mountain-masses, or one of the remnant of the people of ʿĀd.
sentences.i: And lo, the wall split open, and out of it came a huge black slave, as if he were a mountain among mountains, or one of the last of the tribe of ʿĀd.
sentences.n: ʿĀd is the ancient people of the Qurʾān (cf. 7:65, 89:6), proverbial for gigantic stature — the comparison marks the slave as monstrous, echoing but darkening the maiden's appearance in Night 6.

sentences.t: وَ فِي يَدِهِ فَرْعٌ مِنْ شَجَرَةٍ خَضْرَاءَ
sentences.tr: wa-fī yadihi farʿun min shajaratin khaḍrāʾa
sentences.l: and in his hand was a branch from a green tree.

sentences.t: وَ قَالَ بِكَلَامٍ مُزْعِجٍ يَا سَمَكُ يَا سَمَكُ أَنْتُمْ عَلَى الْعَهْدِ الْقَدِيمِ مُقِيمِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla bi-kalāmin muzʿijin yā samaku yā samaku antum ʿalā al-ʿahdi al-qadīmi muqīmīna
sentences.l: and he said, in disturbing speech, "O fish, O fish, are you abiding by the old covenant?"
sentences.i: and he said, in a harsh, unsettling voice, "O fish, O fish! Do you still stand by the old covenant?"
sentences.n: The slave repeats almost verbatim the maiden's challenge from the end of Night 6 — the same uncanny test, now put by a different, more fearsome figure.

sentences.t: وَالسَّمَكُ شَالُوا رُؤُسَهُمْ مِنَ الطَّاجِنِ وَقَالُوا نَعَمْ نَعَمْ نَحْنُ عَلَى الْعَهْدِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-samaku shālū ruʾūsahum mina al-ṭājini wa-qālū naʿam naʿam naḥnu ʿalā al-ʿahdi
sentences.l: and the fish raised their heads from the pan and said, "Yes, yes — we are upon the covenant."
sentences.i: and the fish lifted their heads from the pan and cried, "Yes! Yes! We stand by the covenant!" —
sentences.n: شَالُوا is colloquial for Classical رَفَعُوا, 'they raised', as already in Night 6. رُؤُسَهُمْ is a contracted spelling of رُؤُوسَهُمْ, 'their heads' — the doubled wāw of the plural collapsed to one, exactly as in Night 6's روسهم.

sentences.t: اِنْ عُدْتَ عُدْنَا وَاِنْ وَافَيْتَ وَافَيْنَا * وَاِنْ هَجَرْتُمْ قَدْ فَاِنَّا تَكَافَيْنَا
sentences.tr: in ʿudta ʿudnā wa-in wāfayta wāfaynā * wa-in hajartum qad fa-innā takāfaynā
sentences.l: If you returned, we returned; and if you kept faith, we kept faith — and if you forsook us, then we, indeed, have matched you in kind.
sentences.i: If you come back, we come back; if you keep faith, so do we; and should you turn away, we too shall surely turn away in kind.
sentences.n: This repeats, with variation, the maiden's verse from the end of Night 6 — the same taunt-and-answer couplet recast for the slave's voice (there ʿultum/tahāfaynā or tadfaynā; here ʿudta/takāfaynā). Note the shift from singular address (ʿudta, wāfayta) to plural (hajartum) within the same couplet, kept as printed. تَكَافَيْنَا, form VI of ك-ف-ي, 'we have requited one another', rhymes on wāfaynā.

sentences.t: وَأَقْبَلَ الْعَبْدُ عَلَى الطَّاجِنِ وَقَلَبَهُ بِالْغُصْنِ الَّذِي فِي يَدِهِ وَخَرَجَ مِنْ مَوْضِعِ مَا أَتَى
sentences.tr: wa-aqbala al-ʿabdu ʿalā al-ṭājini wa-qalabahu bi-al-ghuṣni alladhī fī yadihi wa-kharaja min mawḍiʿi mā atā
sentences.l: And the slave turned to the pan and overturned it with the branch that was in his hand, and went out from the place from which he had come.
sentences.i: Then the slave turned upon the pan and overturned it with the branch in his hand, and went out the way he had come.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ الْوَزِيرُ وَالْمَلِكُ إِلَى السَّمَكِ فَرَأَوْهُ صَارَ مِثْلَ الْفَحِيمِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara al-wazīru wa-al-maliku ilā al-samaki fa-raʾawhu ṣāra mithla al-faḥīmi
sentences.l: Then the vizier and the king looked at the fish, and saw it had become like the charcoal.
sentences.i: Then the vizier and the king looked at the fish and saw that it had turned to charcoal.
sentences.n: الْفَحِيمِ stands where الْفَحْمِ, 'charcoal', would be expected — perhaps an intensive or dialectal variant (faḥīm, 'glowing coal'); kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَتَدَهَّلَ الْمَلِكُ وَقَالَ هَذَا أَمْرٌ لَا يُمْكِنُ السُّكُوتُ عَنْهُ وَإِنَّ هَذَا السَّمَكَ لَهُ شَأْنٌ
sentences.tr: fa-tadahhala al-maliku wa-qāla hādhā amrun lā yumkinu al-sukūtu ʿanhu wa-inna hādhā al-samaka lahu shaʾnun
sentences.l: Then the king was astounded, and said, "This is a matter about which silence is not possible, and indeed this fish has some affair of its own."
sentences.i: The king was dumbfounded, and said, "This is a thing that cannot be passed over in silence — there is something strange about this fish."
sentences.n: تَدَهَّلَ, 'to be astounded, thrown into confusion', is an unusual form V verb from د-ه-ل, kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَأَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ بِإِحْضَارِ الصَّيَّادِ فَلَمَّا حَضَرَ قَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ وَيْلَكَ مِنْ أَيْنَ هَذَا السَّمَكُ
sentences.tr: fa-amara al-maliku bi-iḥḍāri al-ṣayyādi fa-lammā ḥaḍara qāla lahu al-maliku waylaka min ayna hādhā al-samaku
sentences.l: So the king ordered the bringing of the fisherman; and when he came, the king said to him, "Woe to you — from where is this fish?"
sentences.i: So the king ordered the fisherman brought before him; and when he came, the king said to him, "Confound you — where does this fish come from?"
sentences.n: وَيْلَكَ, 'woe to you', is a mild exclamation of impatience or alarm here, not a real curse.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ مِنْ بِرْكَةٍ بَيْنَ أَرْبَعِ جِبَالٍ تَحْتَ هَذَا الْجَبَلِ الَّذِي بِظَاهِرِ مَدِينَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu min birkatin bayna arbaʿi jibālin taḥta hādhā al-jabali alladhī bi-ẓāhiri madīnatika
sentences.l: So he said to him, "From a pool between four mountains, beneath this mountain that is at the outskirts of your city."
sentences.i: He said to him, "From a pool between four mountains, beneath this very mountain at the edge of your city."

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى الصَّيَّادِ وَقَالَ مَسِيرَةُ كَمْ يَوْمٍ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata al-maliku ilā al-ṣayyādi wa-qāla masīratu kam yawmin
sentences.l: Then the king turned to the fisherman and said, "A journey of how many days?"
sentences.i: The king turned to the fisherman and said, "How many days' journey is it?"

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ يَا مَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانُ مَسِيرَةُ نِصْفِ سَاعَةٍ
sentences.tr: qāla lahu yā mawlānā al-sulṭānu masīratu niṣfi sāʿatin
sentences.l: He said to him, "O our lord the Sultan, a journey of half an hour."
sentences.i: He answered him, "O our lord the Sultan, it is but half an hour's journey."

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ السُّلْطَانُ وَأَمَرَ بِخُرُوجِ الْعَسْكَرِ وَرُكُوبِ الْجَيْشِ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-sulṭānu wa-amara bi-khurūji al-ʿaskari wa-rukūbi al-jayshi min waqtihi
sentences.l: The Sultan marveled, and ordered the going-forth of the army and the mounting of the troops, from his moment.
sentences.i: The Sultan marveled, and gave orders for the army to march out and the troops to mount, that very hour.
sentences.n: مِنْ وَقْتِهِ, 'from his own moment', is the fixed idiom for 'at once, immediately' (cf. مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ in Night 6).

sentences.t: وَالصَّيَّادُ مَعَهُ قُدَّامَهُ يَلْعَنُ الْعِفْرِيتَ إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعُوا الْجَبَلَ وَنَزَلُوا إِلَى بَرِّيَّةٍ مُتَّسِعَةٍ لَمْ يَرَوْهَا مُدَّةَ عُمْرِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-al-ṣayyādu maʿahu quddāmahu yalʿanu al-ʿifrīta ilā an ṭalaʿū al-jabala wa-nazalū ilā barriyyatin muttasiʿatin lam yarawhā muddata ʿumrihim
sentences.l: — with the fisherman along with him, before him, cursing the efrit — until they climbed the mountain and went down into a wide wilderness they had not seen in the whole span of their lives.
sentences.i: — the fisherman going with him, ahead of him, cursing the efrit all the way — until they climbed the mountain and descended into a broad wasteland the like of which they had never seen in all their lives.

sentences.t: وَالسُّلْطَانُ وَجَمِيعُ الْعَسْكَرِ يَتَعَجَّبُونَ فَنَظَرُوا تِلْكَ الْبَرِّيَّةَ وَالْبِرْكَةَ فِي وَسَطِهَا بَيْنَ أَرْبَعِ جِبَالٍ وَ السَّمَكَ فِيهَا أَرْبَعَةُ أَلْوَانٍ أَحْمَرُ وَأَبْيَضُ وَأَصْفَرُ وَأَزْرَقُ
sentences.tr: wa-al-sulṭānu wa-jamīʿu al-ʿaskari yataʿajjabūna fa-naẓarū tilka al-barriyyata wa-al-birkata fī wasaṭihā bayna arbaʿi jibālin wa-al-samaka fīhā arbaʿatu alwānin aḥmaru wa-abyaḍu wa-aṣfaru wa-azraqu
sentences.l: with the Sultan and all the army marveling; and they beheld that wilderness, and the pool in its midst between four mountains, and the fish in it — four colors: red, and white, and yellow, and blue.
sentences.i: the Sultan and the whole army marveling as they went — and they looked upon that wilderness, and the pool at its center between the four mountains, with fish of four colors in it: red, white, yellow, and blue.
sentences.n: فَنَظَرُوا تِلْكَ الْبَرِّيَّةَ takes its object directly, without a preposition (Classical would expect نَظَرُوا إِلَى) — a loose Middle Arabic government, as elsewhere in this text (cf. Night 6's قَرُبَ مَدِينَتَهُ).

sentences.t: فَوَقَفَ الْمَلِكُ وَتَعَجَّبَ وَقَٰلَ لِلْعَسْكَرِ وَلِمَنْ حَضَرَ هَلْ أَحَدٌ مِنْكُمْ رَأَى هَذِهِ الْبِرْكَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-waqafa al-maliku wa-taʿajjaba wa-qāla li-al-ʿaskari wa-li-man ḥaḍara hal aḥadun minkum raʾā hādhihi al-birkata
sentences.l: Then the king stopped, and marveled, and said to the army and to whoever was present, "Has anyone among you seen this pool —
sentences.i: Then the king halted, marveling, and said to the army and to all who were present, "Has any one of you ever seen this pool before —
sentences.n: The edition prints قل for قَالَ here, the same defective spelling (missing alif) seen elsewhere in the text; pointed with the dagger alif (قَٰلَ) to preserve the rasm while reading qāla. The king's question breaks off mid-quotation — the answer belongs to the next slice.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا أَبَدًا يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ مُدَّةَ عُمُرِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālū abadan yā malika al-zamāni muddata ʿumrinā
sentences.l: So they said, "Never, O King of the Age, the span of our life."
sentences.i: They said, "Never, O King of the Age, in all the days of our life."
sentences.n: أَبَدًا here stands alone as an emphatic "never," with the negation understood from the question just put to them ("has any of you ever seen this pool?") rather than spelled out with lā or mā.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلُوا مِنَ الطَّاعِنِينَ فِي السِّنِّ فَقَالُوا عُمُرَنَا مَا رَأَيْنَا هَذِهِ الْبِرْكَةَ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾalū mina al-ṭāʿinīna fī al-sinni fa-qālū ʿumranā mā raʾaynā hādhihi al-birkata fī hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: So they asked those advanced in age, and they said, "Our life — we have not seen this pool in this place."
sentences.i: So they asked those of them well on in years, and they too said, "Never in our lives have we seen this pool in this place."

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ وَاللَّهِ لَا أَدْخُلُ مَدِينَتِي وَلَا أَجْلِسُ عَلَى تَخْتِ مُلْكِي حَتَّى أَعْرِفَ أَمْرَ هَذِهِ الْبِرْكَةِ وَهَذَا السَّمَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku wa-Allāhi lā adkhulu madīnatī wa-lā ajlisu ʿalā takhti mulkī ḥattā aʿrifa amra hādhihi al-birkati wa-hādhā al-samaki
sentences.l: So the king said, "By God, I will not enter my city, nor will I sit upon the throne of my kingdom, until I know the matter of this pool and this fish."
sentences.i: Then the king said, "By God, I will not enter my city, nor sit upon the throne of my kingdom, until I learn the secret of this pool and this fish."

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَ النَّاسَ بِالنُّزُولِ حَوْلَ هَذِهِ الْجِبَالِ
sentences.tr: thumma amara al-nāsa bi-al-nuzūli ḥawla hādhihi al-jibāli
sentences.l: Then he ordered the people to the encamping around these mountains.
sentences.i: Then he ordered the people to make camp around these mountains.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَعَى بِالْوَزِيرِ وَكَانَ وَزِيرًا خَبِيرًا عَاقِلًا لَبِيبًا عَالِمًا بِالْأُمُورِ فَحَضَرَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma daʿā bi-al-wazīri wa-kāna wazīran khabīran ʿāqilan labīban ʿāliman bi-al-umūri fa-ḥaḍara bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: Then he called for the vizier — and he was a vizier knowing, wise, intelligent, learned in affairs — and he presented himself between his two hands.
sentences.i: Then he sent for the vizier — a vizier who was knowledgeable, sound of judgment, sharp-witted, and versed in affairs — and he came and stood before him.
sentences.n: دَعَى spells daʿā with final yāʾ (alif maqṣūra) rather than tall alif — an ordinary spelling variant of this hollow-final verb, not a dropped letter, so it needs no dagger alif.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ إِنِّي أَحْبَبْتُ أَنْ أَعْمَلَ شَيًا وَأُخْبِرَكَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu innī aḥbabtu an aʿmala shayan wa-ukhbiraka bihi
sentences.l: So he said to him, "Indeed I have wished that I do a thing and inform you of it."
sentences.i: He said to him, "I have resolved on a thing, and I wish to tell you of it."
sentences.n: شَيًا stands for شَيْئًا, shayʾan, "a thing," printed here without its hamza letter altogether — the same kind of defective spelling as مُسِيًا for مُسِيء in Night 6; the missing consonant is not restored, only the surviving letters are vocalized.

sentences.t: وَ خَطَرَ بِبَالِي أَنْ أَنْفَرِدَ بِنَفْسِي فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَ أَبْحَثَ عَنْ خَبَرِ هَذِهِ الْبِرْكَةِ وَهَذَا السَّمَكِ
sentences.tr: wa-khaṭara bi-bālī an anfarida bi-nafsī fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-abḥatha ʿan khabari hādhihi al-birkati wa-hādhā al-samaki
sentences.l: And it occurred to my mind that I go apart by myself this night and search out the news of this pool and this fish.
sentences.i: It has occurred to me to go off by myself this very night and find out the truth of this pool and this fish.

sentences.t: فَاجْلِسْ أَنْتَ عَلَى بَابِ خَيْمَتِي وَقُلْ لِلْأُمَرَاءِ وَ الْوُزَرَاءِ وَالْحُجَّابِ وَالنُّوَّابِ وَكُلِّ مَنْ سَأَلَ عَنِّي أَنَّ السُّلْطَانَ مُتَوَعِّكٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ijlis anta ʿalā bābi khaymatī wa-qul li-al-umarāʾi wa-al-wuzarāʾi wa-al-ḥujjābi wa-al-nuwwābi wa-kulli man saʾala ʿannī anna al-sulṭāna mutawaʿʿikun
sentences.l: So you sit at the door of my tent, and say to the emirs and the viziers and the chamberlains and the deputies, and everyone who asks about me, that the Sultan is unwell.
sentences.i: So sit yourself at the door of my tent, and tell the emirs, the viziers, the chamberlains, the deputies, and anyone who asks after me, that the Sultan is indisposed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَنِي أَنْ لَا أُعْطِيَ أَحَدًا دُسْتُورًا بِالدُّخُولِ عَلَيْهِ وَلَا تُعْلِمْ أَحَدًا بِقَصْدِي
sentences.tr: wa-amaranī an lā uʿṭiya aḥadan dustūran bi-al-dukhūli ʿalayhi wa-lā tuʿlim aḥadan bi-qaṣdī
sentences.l: And he ordered me that I not give anyone permission to come in upon him, and do not inform anyone of my intent.
sentences.i: And he has ordered me to give no one leave to come in to him — and you are not to let anyone know of my purpose, either.

sentences.t: فَمَا قَدَرَ الْوَزِيرُ أَنْ يُخَالِفَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-mā qadara al-wazīru an yukhālifahu
sentences.l: So the vizier was not able to oppose him.
sentences.i: The vizier was in no position to disobey him.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ غَيَّرَ حِلْيَتَهُ وَتَقَلَّدَ بِسَيْفِهِ وَتَسَلَّقَ مِنْ عَلَى وَاحِدٍ مِنَ الْجِبَالِ وَمَشَى بَقِيَّةَ لَيْلَتِهِ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika ghayyara ḥilyatahu wa-taqallada bi-sayfihi wa-tasallaqa min ʿalā wāḥidin mina al-jibāli wa-mashā baqiyyata laylatihi ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: Then indeed the king changed his guise, and girded himself with his sword, and climbed from atop one of the mountains, and walked the rest of his night until morning.
sentences.i: Then the king changed his dress, girded on his sword, climbed up and over one of the mountains, and walked the rest of that night until morning.
sentences.n: مِنْ عَلَى stacks two prepositions where Classical usage would use one alone — a Middle Arabic habit met already in the frame story's إِلَى عِنْدَ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَشَى يَوْمَهُ كُلَّهُ وَقَدِ اشْتَدَّ عَلَيْهِ الْحَرُّ بِمَشْيِهِ يَوْمَهُ وَلَيْلَتَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma mashā yawmahu kullahu wa-qadi ishtadda ʿalayhi al-ḥarru bi-mashyihi yawmahu wa-laylatahu
sentences.l: Then he walked his whole day, the heat having grown intense upon him from his walking his day and his night.
sentences.i: Then he walked the whole of the next day, the heat growing fierce on him from walking through both day and night.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَشَى اللَّيْلَةَ الثَّانِيَةَ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ فَلَاحَ لَهُ سَوَادٌ مِنْ بَعِيدٍ فَفَرِحَ
sentences.tr: thumma mashā al-laylata al-thāniyata ilā al-ṣabāḥi fa-lāḥa lahu sawādun min baʿīdin fa-fariḥa
sentences.l: Then he walked the second night until morning, and a blackness appeared to him from afar, and he rejoiced.
sentences.i: Then he walked through the second night until morning, when something dark showed itself in the distance, and he was glad.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَعَلِّي أَجِدُ مَنْ يُخْبِرُنِي بِقَضِيَّةِ الْبِرْكَةِ وَالسَّمَكِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla laʿallī ajidu man yukhbirunī bi-qaḍiyyati al-birkati wa-al-samaki
sentences.l: And he said, "Perhaps I shall find one who will tell me of the matter of the pool and the fish."
sentences.i: He said, "Perhaps I shall find someone to tell me the truth of this pool and this fish."

sentences.t: فَتَقَرَّبَ فَوَجَدَ قَصْرًا مَبْنِيًّا بِالْحِجَارَةِ السُّودِ مُصَفَّحًا بِالْحَدِيدِ وَبَابُهُ فَرْدَةٌ مَفْتُوحَةٌ وَ فَرْدَةٌ مَغْلُوقَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-taqarraba fa-wajada qaṣran mabniyyan bi-al-ḥijārati al-sūdi muṣaffaḥan bi-al-ḥadīdi wa-bābuhu fardatun maftūḥatun wa-fardatun maghlūqatun
sentences.l: So he drew near, and found a castle built of the black stones, plated with iron, its door one leaf open and one leaf shut.
sentences.i: So he drew nearer, and found a castle built of black stone and plated with iron, one leaf of its door standing open and the other closed.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ الْمَلِكُ وَوَقَفَ عَلَى الْبَابِ وَدَقَّ دَقًّا لَطِيفًا فَلَمْ يَسْمَعْ جَوَابًا
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa al-maliku wa-waqafa ʿalā al-bābi wa-daqqa daqqan laṭīfan fa-lam yasmaʿ jawāban
sentences.l: So the king rejoiced, and stood at the door, and knocked a gentle knock, but he heard no answer.
sentences.i: The king rejoiced, and stood at the door, and knocked gently — but he heard no answer.

sentences.t: فَدَقَّ ثَانِيًا وَثَالِثًا فَلَمْ يَسْمَعْ جَوَابًا
sentences.tr: fa-daqqa thāniyan wa-thālithan fa-lam yasmaʿ jawāban
sentences.l: So he knocked a second time and a third, but he heard no answer.
sentences.i: So he knocked again, and a third time, but heard no answer.

sentences.t: فَدَقَّ دَقًّا مُزْعِجًا فَلَمْ يُجِبْهُ أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: fa-daqqa daqqan muzʿijan fa-lam yujibhu aḥadun
sentences.l: So he knocked a violent knock, but no one answered him.
sentences.i: So he knocked violently — but still no one answered him.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَا شَكَّ أَنَّهُ خَالٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lā shakka annahu khālin
sentences.l: So he said, "No doubt it is empty."
sentences.i: So he said to himself, "No doubt it stands empty."

sentences.t: فَشَجَّعَ نَفْسَهُ وَدَخَلَ مِنْ بَابِ الْقَصْرِ إِلَى دِهْلِيزٍ
sentences.tr: fa-shajjaʿa nafsahu wa-dakhala min bābi al-qaṣri ilā dihlīzin
sentences.l: So he took courage for himself, and entered from the gate of the castle into a vestibule.
sentences.i: So he steeled himself, and passed in through the castle gate into an entrance hall.

sentences.t: وَصَرَخَ وَقَالَ يَا أَهْلَ الْقَصْرِ رَجُلٌ غَرِيبٌ وَعَابِرُ سَبِيلٍ هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ شَيٌ مِنَ الزَّادِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣarakha wa-qāla yā ahla al-qaṣri rajulun gharībun wa-ʿābiru sabīlin hal ʿindakum shayun mina al-zādi
sentences.l: And he cried out and said, "O people of the castle, a strange man and a passer of the way — is there with you anything of provisions?"
sentences.i: And he called out, saying, "O people of the castle! A stranger and a wayfarer asks: have you any provisions to spare?"
sentences.n: شَيٌ stands for شَيْءٌ, shayʾun, with the hamza letter dropped from the print, exactly as شَيًا earlier in this same slice.

sentences.t: وَأَعَادَ الْقَوْلَ ثَانِيًا وَثَالِثًا فَلَمْ يَسْمَعْ جَوَابًا
sentences.tr: wa-aʿāda al-qawla thāniyan wa-thālithan fa-lam yasmaʿ jawāban
sentences.l: And he repeated the saying a second time and a third, but he heard no answer.
sentences.i: He repeated his words a second time, and a third, but heard no answer.

sentences.t: فَقَوَّى نَفْسَهُ وَثَبَّتَ جَنَانَهُ وَدَخَلَ مِنَ الدَّهَالِيزِ إِلَى وَسَطِ الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qawwā nafsahu wa-thabbata janānahu wa-dakhala mina al-dahālīzi ilā wasaṭi al-qaṣri
sentences.l: So he strengthened himself, and steadied his heart, and passed on from the passages into the middle of the castle.
sentences.i: So he braced himself and steadied his heart, and made his way on through the passages into the heart of the castle.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا يَجِدُ فِيهِ أَثَاثًا غَيْرَ أَنَّهُ مَفْرُوشٌ بِالْحَرِيرِ وَالْأَنْطَاعِ الْمُلُوكِيَّةِ وَالسَّتَائِرِ الْمُرْخَاةِ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā yajidu fīhi athāthan ghayra annahu mafrūshun bi-al-ḥarīri wa-al-anṭāʿi al-mulūkiyyati wa-al-satāʾiri al-murkhāti
sentences.l: And behold, he finds in it furnishings — except that it is spread with silk, and the royal hides, and the loosed curtains.
sentences.i: And there, to his eyes, it was furnished throughout — hung with silk, royal hides, and curtains let down all about.
sentences.n: غَيْرَ أَنَّهُ reads oddly here as a strict "except that"; it is taken as loosely introducing what the furnishings consisted of (silk, hides, curtains) rather than contrasting with an unstated negative, though the sentence may be compressed or slightly disordered in the print.

sentences.t: وَ فِي وَسَطِ الْقَصْرِ رَحْبَةٌ وَ أَرْبَعَةُ أَوَاوِينَ وَ مِصْطَبَةٌ وَ إِيوَانٌ قُبَالَ إِيوَانٍ وَ شَاذَرْوَانٌ وَ فِسْقِيَّةٌ عَلَيْهَا أَرْبَعُ سِبَاعٍ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ الْأَحْمَرِ تُلْقِي الْمَاءَ مِنْ أَفْوَاهِهَا كَالدُّرِّ وَالْجَوْهَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī wasaṭi al-qaṣri raḥbatun wa-arbaʿatu awāwīna wa-miṣṭabatun wa-īwānun qubāla īwānin wa-shādharwānun wa-fisqiyyatun ʿalayhā arbaʿu sibāʿin mina al-dhahabi al-aḥmari tulqī al-māʾa min afwāhihā ka-al-durri wa-al-jawhari
sentences.l: And in the middle of the castle was an open court, and four iwans, and a dais, and an iwan facing an iwan, and a marble runnel, and a fountain-basin, upon it four lions of red gold casting the water from their mouths like pearl and gem.
sentences.i: And in the heart of the castle was an open court, four vaulted iwans, a raised dais, an iwan facing an iwan, a marble runnel, and a fountain-basin bearing four lions of red gold that poured water from their mouths like pearls and jewels.
sentences.n: An iwan (إِيوَان) is a vaulted hall open on one side onto a court; شَاذَرْوَان is a Persian loanword for the sloped, ribbed marble channel that carries a fountain's water. تُلْقِي, feminine singular, agrees with سِبَاع as a non-human plural, in the pattern already met in the frame story (شَبَابِيكُ تُطِلُّ).

sentences.t: وَدَائِرَ الْقَصْرِ طُيُورٌ وَ عَلَى الْقَصْرِ شَبَكَةٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ تَمْنَعُهُمْ مِنَ الطُّلُوعِ
sentences.tr: wa-dāʾira al-qaṣri ṭuyūrun wa-ʿalā al-qaṣri shabakatun mina al-dhahabi tamnaʿuhum mina al-ṭulūʿi
sentences.l: And around the castle were birds, and over the castle was a netting of gold, keeping them from the going-up.
sentences.i: And birds circled the castle on every side, and over it was stretched a golden net that kept them from flying up and away.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَرَ أَحَدًا فَتَعَجَّبَ الْمَلِكُ وَ تَأَسَّفَ لِكَوْنِهِ لَمْ يَرَ أَحَدًا يَسْتَخْبِرُ مِنْهُ عَنْ تِلْكَ الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَ الْبِرْكَةِ وَالسَّمَكِ وَالْجِبَالِ وَالْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yara aḥadan fa-taʿajjaba al-maliku wa-taʾassafa li-kawnihi lam yara aḥadan yastakhbiru minhu ʿan tilka al-barriyyati wa-al-birkati wa-al-samaki wa-al-jibāli wa-al-qaṣri
sentences.l: But he saw no one; so the king marveled, and grieved at his not seeing anyone to ask of, concerning that wilderness, and the pool, and the fish, and the mountains, and the castle.
sentences.i: But he found no one there; and the king was amazed, and grieved that he had found no one of whom he might ask about that wilderness, and the pool, and the fish, and the mountains, and the castle.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَلَسَ بَيْنَ الْأَبْوَابِ يَتَفَكَّرُ
sentences.tr: thumma jalasa bayna al-abwābi yatafakkaru
sentences.l: Then he sat between the doors, pondering.
sentences.i: Then he sat down between the doors, lost in thought.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا هُوَ بِأَنِينٍ مِنْ كَبِدٍ حَزِينٍ وَهُوَ يَتَرَنَّمُ وَيَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā huwa bi-anīnin min kabidin ḥazīnin wa-huwa yatarannamu wa-yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: And behold, there was with him a groaning from a grieved heart, one chanting and saying, in verse:
sentences.i: And all at once he heard the groan of a grieving heart, someone chanting low and reciting, in verse:
sentences.n: شِعْرٌ closes the sentence as the manuscript's own rubric introducing the verse that follows (rather than a grammatical accusative object of يَقُولُ), printed with no final alif; it is pointed here as an indeclinable label rather than forcing an accusative tanwīn the spelling does not support.

sentences.t: اَخْفَيْتُ مَا القَاهُ بِي وَقَدْ ظَهَرْ * وَالنَّوْمُ مِنْ عَيْنِي تَبَدَّلَ بِالسَّهَرْ
sentences.tr: akhfaytu mā alqāhu bī wa-qad ẓahar * wa-al-nawmu min ʿaynī tabaddala bi-al-sahar
sentences.l: I hid what it cast upon me, though it has shown itself * and sleep, from my eye, was exchanged for wakefulness.
sentences.i: I hid what fate had inflicted on me, yet it has come to light; and sleep has fled my eyes, exchanged for sleeplessness.
sentences.n: القَاهُ stands for أَلْقَاهُ (form IV of أَلْقَى, 'to cast, inflict') + -hu, 'it' — the implied subject being Time/Fate, addressed directly in the next line; its hamza is spelled as a plain alif, as often in this edition. The poem that follows is a conventional lover's lament of concealed grief and fate's cruelty, its six lines monorhymed on -ar; the king overhears it being recited before he traces the voice.

sentences.t: يَا دَهْرُ لَا تُبْقِي عَلَيَّ وَلَا تَذَرْ * هَا مِحْنَتِي بَيْنَ الْمَشَقَّةِ وَالْخَطَرْ
sentences.tr: yā dahru lā tubqī ʿalayya wa-lā tadhar * hā miḥnatī bayna al-mashaqqati wa-al-khaṭar
sentences.l: O Time, you do not spare me, nor do you leave off * here is my ordeal, between hardship and peril.
sentences.i: O Time, you spare no one, and you never let go — behold my ordeal, caught between hardship and peril.
sentences.n: لَا تُبْقِي وَلَا تَذَرْ echoes the Qur'anic description of Hellfire (Q. 74:28, لَا تُبْقِي وَلَا تَذَرُ, 'it spares not, nor does it leave anything'), turned here into an apostrophe to personified Time.

sentences.t: مَا تَرْحَمُونَ عَزِيزَ قَوْمٍ ذَلَّ فِي * شَرْعِ الْهَوَى وَغَنِيَّ قَوْمٍ افْتَقَرْ
sentences.tr: mā tarḥamūna ʿazīza qawmin dhalla fī * sharʿi al-hawā wa-ghaniyya qawmin iftaqar
sentences.l: You show no mercy to the mighty one of a people, abased in * the law of passion, and the wealthy one of a people, impoverished.
sentences.i: You show no pity for the once-mighty man of his people, brought low by love's law, nor for the once-rich man of his people, left poor.

sentences.t: كُنَّا نَغَارُ مِنَ النَّسِيمِ عَلَيْكُمُ * لَكِنْ اذَا نَزَلَ الْقَضَا عَمِيَ الْبَصَرْ
sentences.tr: kunnā naghāru mina al-nasīmi ʿalaykumu * lākin idhā nazala al-qaḍā ʿamiya al-baṣar
sentences.l: We used to be jealous, of the breeze, over you * but when the decree descends, the eye goes blind.
sentences.i: We used to envy even the breeze that touched you; but when fate's decree comes down, the eye is blinded.

sentences.t: مَا حِيلَةُ الرَّامِي اذَا الْتَفَّتِ الْعُلَا * فَارَادَ يَرْمِي السَّهْمَ فَنْقَطَعَ الْوَتَرْ
sentences.tr: mā ḥīlatu al-rāmī idhā iltaffati al-ʿulā * fa-arāda yarmī al-sahma fa-nqaṭaʿa al-watar
sentences.l: What recourse has the archer, when the heights close in * and he means to loose the arrow, and the bowstring snaps?
sentences.i: What can the archer do, when the coils of fortune close in around him, and, just as he would loose the arrow, the bowstring snaps?
sentences.n: الْعُلَا ('the heights, the exalted things') is left elliptical in the Arabic; it is taken here as a figure for encircling adversity. The image of an archer thwarted at the very instant of the shot, his string snapping, is a stock figure for fate defeating skill and effort.

sentences.t: وَاذَا تَشَتَّتِ الْهُمُومُ عَلَى الْفَتَى * اَيْنَ الْمَفَرُّ مِنَ الْقَضَا وَمِنَ الْقَدَرْ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā tashattati al-humūmu ʿalā al-fatā * ayna al-mafarru mina al-qaḍā wa-mina al-qadar
sentences.l: And when cares scatter over the young man * where is the escape, from decree and from destiny?
sentences.i: And when cares descend on a young man from every side, where is there refuge from fate and from destiny?

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ السُّلْطَانُ الْأَنِينَ نَهَضَ قَائِمًا وَ تَبِعَ الْحِسَّ فَوَجَدَ سِتْرًا مُرْخًى عَلَى بَابِ مَجْلِسٍ فَشَالَ السِّتْرَ فَرَأَى خَلْفَهُ شَابًّا جَالِسًا عَلَى سَرِيرٍ مُرْتَفِعٍ عَنِ الْأَرْضِ مِقْدَارَ ذِرَاعٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-sulṭānu al-anīna nahaḍa qāʾiman wa-tabiʿa al-ḥissa fa-wajada sitran murkhan ʿalā bābi majlisin fa-shāla al-sitra fa-raʾā khalfahu shābban jālisan ʿalā sarīrin murtafiʿin ʿani al-arḍi miqdāra dhirāʿin
sentences.l: And when the Sultan heard the groaning, he rose up standing and followed the sound; and he found a curtain let-down over the door of a chamber; so he lifted the curtain and saw, behind it, a young man sitting on a couch raised above the ground the measure of a forearm.
sentences.i: When the Sultan heard the groaning, he rose to his feet and followed the sound, and found a curtain drawn across the doorway of a chamber. He lifted the curtain and saw, behind it, a young man seated on a couch raised a cubit's height above the ground.
sentences.n: شَالَ ('lifted') is the same Middle Arabic verb for 'to raise, lift' (standing in for Classical رَفَعَ) met before in this narrative Arabic — here of lifting a curtain. Hamza is supplied editorially on الْأَنِينَ and الْأَرْضِ, printed bare in the archive.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ شَبٌّ مَلِيحٌ بِقَدٍّ رَجِيحٍ وَلِسَانٍ فَصِيحٍ وَ جَبِينٍ أَزْهَرَ وَخَدٍّ أَحْمَرَ وَ شَامَةٍ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّ خَدِّهِ كَقُرْصِ عَنْبَرٍ كَمَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa shabbun malīḥun bi-qaddin rajīḥin wa-lisānin faṣīḥin wa-jabīnin azhara wa-khaddin aḥmara wa-shāmatin ʿalā kursiyyi khaddihi ka-qurṣi ʿanbarin kamā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And he (was) a youth, handsome, of well-balanced stature and eloquent tongue and radiant brow and red cheek, and a mole on the throne of his cheek like a disc of ambergris — as the poet said:
sentences.i: He was a handsome youth, of graceful stature and eloquent tongue, radiant of brow and red of cheek, with a mole upon his cheek like a disc of ambergris — as the poet said:
sentences.n: The description runs as sajʿ (rhymed prose): مَلِيحٌ … رَجِيحٍ … فَصِيحٍ chime on -īḥ, then أَزْهَرَ … أَحْمَرَ on -ar. شَبٌّ here (spelled without alif) is the same word as شَابًّا two clauses earlier (spelled with it) — a Middle Arabic spelling doublet for 'young man', kept as printed in both places. كُرْسِيِّ خَدِّهِ, literally 'the throne/seat of his cheek', simply means 'on his very cheek'. Hamza is supplied editorially on أَزْهَرَ and أَحْمَرَ, printed bare in the archive.

sentences.t: وَمُهَفْهَفٍ مِنْ شَعْرِهِ وَجَبِينِهِ * تُمْسِي الوَرَى فِي ظُلْمَةٍ وَضِيَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-muhafhafin min shaʿrihi wa-jabīnihi * tumsī al-warā fī ẓulmatin wa-ḍiyāʾi
sentences.l: And many a slender one, by his hair and his brow * mankind spends the evening in darkness and light.
sentences.i: And many a slender youth, by his hair and his brow, leaves mankind each evening between darkness and radiance.
sentences.n: The line opens on a bare indefinite genitive (وَمُهَفْهَفٍ), the common poetic ellipsis of رُبَّ, 'many a...'. The conceit plays black hair against a bright forehead: humankind, gazing on him, passes at once through nightfall and daylight.

sentences.t: لَا تُنْكِرُوا الْحَالَ الَّذِي فِي خَدِّهِ * كُلُّ الشَّقِيقِ بِنُقْطَةٍ سَوْدَاءِ
sentences.tr: lā tunkirū al-ḥāla alladhī fī khaddihi * kullu al-shaqīqi bi-nuqṭatin sawdāʾi
sentences.l: Do not deny the mark that is on his cheek * every anemone has a black dot.
sentences.i: Do not hold his cheek's mark against him — every red anemone carries its own black dot.
sentences.n: الْحَالَ ('state, condition') is used loosely here for 'mark, token', referring back to the mole (شَامَة) the prose has just described. The couplet defends the young man's mole by comparing it to the natural black centre of the red anemone flower (الشَّقِيق) — a stock conceit answering an unspoken objection to a beloved's blemish.

sentences.t: فَرِحَ الْمَلِكُ حِينَ رَآهُ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fariḥa al-maliku ḥīna raʾāhu wa-sallama ʿalayhi
sentences.l: The king rejoiced when he saw him, and greeted him.
sentences.i: The king was overjoyed at the sight of him, and gave him greeting.

sentences.t: وَالصَّبِيُّ جَالِسٌ وَعَلَيْهِ قَبَاءُ حَرِيرٍ بِطَرَائِزَ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ الْمِصْرِيِّ وَفَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ تَاجٌ مُكَلَّلٌ بِالْجَوَاهِرِ وَلَكِنَّهُ عَلَيْهِ أَثَرُ الْحُزْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-ṣabiyyu jālisun wa-ʿalayhi qabāʾu ḥarīrin bi-ṭarāʾiza mina al-dhahabi al-miṣriyyi wa-fawqa raʾsihi tājun mukallalun bi-al-jawāhiri wa-lākinnahu ʿalayhi atharu al-ḥuzni
sentences.l: The youth sitting there, and upon him a robe of silk with borders of Egyptian gold, and above his head a crown studded with jewels — but upon him was the mark of sorrow.
sentences.i: The young man sat there in a silk robe trimmed with bands of Egyptian gold, a jewelled crown upon his head — yet the mark of sorrow showed plainly on him.
sentences.n: قَبَاء is a long silk caftan/robe of honour, and طَرَائِز are ornamental bands or trimmings — courtly dress marking him as a king. This whole clause is a circumstantial (ḥāl) description of the youth as the king found him, interrupting the greeting begun in the previous unit.

sentences.t: فَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ الْمَلِكُ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ بِأَحْسَنِ سَلَامٍ وَ قَالَ يَا سَيِّدِي أَنْتَ أَعَزُّ مِنَ الْغَمَامِ وَلِيَ الْمَعْذِرَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-sallama ʿalayhi al-maliku fa-radda ʿalayhi bi-aḥsani salāmin wa-qāla yā sayyidī anta aʿazzu mina al-ghamāmi wa-liya al-maʿdhiratu
sentences.l: So the king greeted him, and he returned to him the finest of greetings, and said, 'O my lord, you are more precious than the clouds — and mine is the excuse.'
sentences.i: The king then gave him greeting, and the young man returned it most graciously, saying, 'My lord, you are more precious than the very rain-clouds — but you must excuse me.'
sentences.n: The greeting named at the start of this passage is completed only here, after the descriptive digression about the youth's appearance — a resumptive fa- picking the action back up, not a duplication. 'أَعَزُّ مِنَ الْغَمَامِ', lit. 'dearer/mightier than the clouds', is an extravagant courtly compliment. 'وَلِيَ الْمَعْذِرَةُ', lit. 'and mine is the excuse', asks pardon without yet saying for what.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ قَدْ عَذَرْتُكَ أَيُّهَا الْفَتَى وَأَنَا ضَيْفٌ عِنْدَكَ وَأَتَيْتُكَ فِي حَاجَةٍ مُهِمَّةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku qad ʿadhartuka ayyuhā al-fatā wa-anā ḍayfun ʿindaka wa-ataytuka fī ḥājatin muhimmatin
sentences.l: So the king said, 'I have excused you, O young man; and I am a guest with you, and I have come to you on an urgent errand.'
sentences.i: The king said, 'I excuse you, young man. I am a guest here with you, and I have come to you with a pressing need.'

sentences.t: أُرِيدُ تُخْبِرَنِي عَنْ هَذِهِ الْبِرْكَةِ وَعَنْ هَذَا السَّمَكِ وَعَنْ هَذَا الْقَصْرِ وَعَنْ سَبَبِ وَحْدَتِكَ فِيهِ وَسَبَبِ بُكَاكَ
sentences.tr: urīdu tukhbiranī ʿan hādhihi al-birkati wa-ʿan hādhā al-samaki wa-ʿan hādhā al-qaṣri wa-ʿan sababi waḥdatika fīhi wa-sababi bukāka
sentences.l: I want [that] you tell me about this pool, and about this fish, and about this castle, and about the reason for your solitude in it, and the reason for your weeping.
sentences.i: I want you to tell me about this pool, this fish, this castle, the reason for your being alone here, and the reason for your weeping.
sentences.n: أَنْ is left unwritten before تُخْبِرَنِي, a colloquial-leaning ellipsis ('I want — you tell me') common in this text's Middle Arabic. بُكَاك is likewise printed without the hamza letter that بُكَائِك would normally carry — the consonant is simply dropped in this spelling, not merely written with a bare alif standing in for it, so nothing is supplied editorially here.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الشَّابُّ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ نَزَلَتْ دُمُوعُهُ عَلَى خُدُودِهِ وَبَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا حَتَّى غَرِقَ صَدْرُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-shābbu hādhā al-kalāma nazalat dumūʿuhu ʿalā khudūdihi wa-bakā bukāʾan shadīdan ḥattā ghariqa ṣadruhu
sentences.l: And when the young man heard this speech, his tears fell down upon his cheeks, and he wept a violent weeping, until his chest was drowned.
sentences.i: When the young man heard this, his tears streamed down his cheeks, and he wept so bitterly that his chest was drenched with tears.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: Then he recited, saying:

sentences.t: قَالُوا لِمَنْ نَامَ الْأَيَّامُ لَهُ رَامَتْ * كَمْ أَقْعَدَتْ نَائِبَاتُ الدَّهْرِ مَنْ قَامَتْ
sentences.tr: qālū li-man nāma al-ayyāmu lahu rāmat * kam aqʿadat nāʾibātu al-dahri man qāmat
sentences.l: They said, of him for whom the Days have slept, they have schemed * How many, who once stood, has Time's misfortunes made to sit down!
sentences.i: They say: against the man who sleeps, the Days lay their schemes * How many who once stood tall has Fortune's turning brought low!
sentences.n: A conventional topos on the treachery of dahr (Time/Fate): heedless ease invites Fate's stroke. The four lines of the two epigrams share a single end-rhyme in -āmat/-ashar-style pairs (here rāmat/qāmat/nāmat/dāmat), a formal feature of this kind of interpolated verse.

sentences.t: إِنْ كُنْتَ نِمْتَ فَعَيْنُ اللَّهِ مَا نَامَتْ * لِمَنْ صَفَا الْوَقْتُ وَالدُّنْيَا لِمَنْ دَامَتْ
sentences.tr: in kunta nimta fa-ʿaynu Allāhi mā nāmat * li-man ṣafā al-waqtu wa-al-dunyā li-man dāmat
sentences.l: If you have slept, [know that] the eye of God has not slept * For whom has time ever been untroubled, and for whom has the world ever lasted?
sentences.i: Though you may sleep, the eye of God never sleeps * For whom has fortune ever stayed serene, or the world ever stood still?

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَنَفَّسَ تَنَفُّسَ الصُّعَدَاءِ وَأَنْشَدَ
sentences.tr: thumma tanaffasa tanaffusa al-ṣuʿadāʾi wa-anshada
sentences.l: Then he breathed the breath of the toiling-uphill, and recited:
sentences.i: Then he heaved a deep, labouring sigh, and recited:
sentences.n: تَنَفُّسُ الصُّعَدَاءِ is a fixed idiom for a long, heavy sigh — literally 'the breathing of one climbing a steep ascent'.

sentences.t: سَلِّمِ الْأَمْرَ إِلَى رَبِّ الْبَشَرْ * وَانْزِلِ الْهَمَّ وَدَعْ عَنْكَ الْفِكَرْ
sentences.tr: sallimi al-amra ilā rabbi al-bashar * wa-anzili al-hamma wa-daʿ ʿanka al-fikar
sentences.l: Surrender the matter to the Lord of mankind * and lay down the worry, and leave off from you the anxious thoughts.
sentences.i: Surrender your affairs to the Lord of all mankind * lay your worry down, and put away your fretting thoughts.
sentences.n: Invokes qaḍāʾ wa-qadar — divine decree and predestination — the standard formula of pious resignation to fate that closes this kind of lament.

sentences.t: لَا تَقُلْ فِيمَا جَرَى كَيْفَ جَرَى * كُلُّ شَيْءٍ بِقَضَاءٍ وَقَدَرْ
sentences.tr: lā taqul fīmā jarā kayfa jarā * kullu shayʾin bi-qaḍāʾin wa-qadar
sentences.l: Do not say, of what came to pass, 'How did it come to pass?' * Everything is by decree and by destiny.
sentences.i: Do not ask of what has happened, 'How did it happen?' * Everything comes by decree and by destiny.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْمَلِكُ وَقَالَ لَهُ مَا يُبْكِيكَ أَيُّهَا الشَّابُّ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-maliku wa-qāla lahu mā yubkīka ayyuhā al-shābbu
sentences.l: Then the king marveled, and said to him: What makes you weep, O young man?
sentences.i: The king marveled, and said to him: What makes you weep, young man?

sentences.t: فَقَالَ كَيْفَ لَا أَبْكِي وَهَذِهِ حَالَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla kayfa lā abkī wa-hādhihi ḥālatī
sentences.l: He said: How should I not weep, when this is my state?
sentences.i: He said: How could I not weep, when this is my condition?

sentences.t: وَمَدَّ يَدَهُ إِلَى أَذْيَالِهِ فَرَفَعَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-madda yadahu ilā adhyālihi fa-rafaʿahā
sentences.l: And he stretched out his hand to his skirts, and lifted them.
sentences.i: And he reached down to the hem of his robe and lifted it.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا هُوَ نِصْفُهُ التَّحْتَانِيُّ حَجَرٌ إِلَى قَدَمَيْهِ وَمِنْ سُرَّتِهِ إِلَى شَعْرِ رَأْسِهِ بَشَرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā huwa niṣfuhu al-taḥtāniyyu ḥajarun ilā qadamayhi wa-min surratihi ilā shaʿri raʾsihi basharun
sentences.l: And behold, he — his lower half was stone down to his feet, and from his navel to the hair of his head was flesh.
sentences.i: And there he was: from the waist down he was stone, down to his very feet, while from his navel to the crown of his head he was living flesh.
sentences.n: The reveal is exact and unsoftened in the Arabic: the young man is quite literally stone below the waist and living flesh above the navel, with the change occurring somewhere across the torso; the subject of the second clause ("flesh") is left understood, in parallel with "his lower half" in the first.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمَلِكُ الشَّابَّ بِهَذِهِ الْحَالَةِ حَزِنَ حُزْنًا عَظِيمًا وَتَأَسَّفَ وَتَأَوَّهَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-maliku al-shābba bi-hādhihi al-ḥālati ḥazina ḥuznan ʿaẓīman wa-taʾassafa wa-taʾawwaha
sentences.l: And when the king saw the young man in this state, he grieved a great grief, and was sorry, and sighed.
sentences.i: When the king saw the young man in this condition, he was overcome with grief, filled with sorrow, and sighed deeply.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَا فَتَى لَقَدْ زِدْتَنِي هَمًّا عَلَى هَمِّي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā fatā laqad zidtanī hamman ʿalā hammī
sentences.l: And he said: O young man, you have indeed added to me sorrow upon my sorrow.
sentences.i: And he said: O young man, you have added yet more grief to my grief.

sentences.t: كُنْتُ أَطْلُبُ السَّمَكَ وَخَبَرَهُ وَصِرْتُ الْأَنَ أَسْأَلُ عَنْ خَبَرِهِ وَخَبَرِكَ
sentences.tr: kuntu aṭlubu al-samaka wa-khabarahu wa-ṣirtu al-āna asʾalu ʿan khabarihi wa-khabarik
sentences.l: I was seeking the fish and its story, and I have come now to ask about its story and your story.
sentences.i: I set out asking after the fish and its story — and now I find myself asking about its story, and yours as well.
sentences.n: The king plays on the double sense of خَبَر ("news, story, affair"): what he first wanted was only the fish's خَبَر; now the young man's own خَبَرَك ("your story" — here really "your condition, what has befallen you") has become an equally urgent unknown.

sentences.t: فَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ
sentences.tr: fa-lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīm
sentences.l: So there is no power and no strength except with God, the High, the Great.
sentences.i: There is no power and no strength save in God, the Most High, the Almighty.
sentences.n: The ḥawqala formula — a set exclamation of dismay or helplessness before what one has just heard or seen.

sentences.t: عَجِّلْ عَلَيَّ يَا فَتَى بِبَثِّ الْحَدِيثِ
sentences.tr: ʿajjil ʿalayya yā fatā bi-baththi al-ḥadīth
sentences.l: Hasten upon me, O young man, with the pouring-out of the account.
sentences.i: Hurry, young man — pour out the story to me.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَعْطِنِي سَمْعَكَ وَ بَصَرَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla aʿṭinī samʿaka wa-baṣarak
sentences.l: He said: Give me your hearing and your sight.
sentences.i: He said: Give me your full attention.
sentences.n: "Give me your ear and your eye" is the idiom for undivided attention; "i" collapses the doublet.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ إِنَّ إِنَّ سَمْعِي وَبَصَرِي حَاضِرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku inna inna samʿī wa-baṣarī ḥāḍirun
sentences.l: So the king said: 'Indeed, indeed — my hearing and my sight are present.'
sentences.i: The king said, 'Indeed — my ears and eyes are yours.'
sentences.n: إِنَّ is printed twice in the archive (ان ان); most likely a compositor's dittography of the single emphatic "indeed," kept here exactly as printed rather than silently reduced to one word.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشَّابُّ إِنَّ لِهَذَا السَّبَبِ وَلِي أَمْرٌ عَجِيبٌ أَوْ كُتِبَ بِالْإِبَرِ عَلَى أَمَاقِ الْبَصَرِ لَكَانَ عِبْرَةً لِمَنِ اعْتَبَرَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shābbu inna li-hādhā al-sababi wa-lī amrun ʿajībun aw kutiba bi-al-ibari ʿalā āmāqi al-baṣari la-kāna ʿibratan li-mani iʿtabar
sentences.l: The young man said: Truly, for this reason I have an amazing matter — or, were it written with needles upon the corners of the eye, it would be a lesson to whoever takes heed.
sentences.i: The young man said: Truly, there lies behind this cause a wondrous matter of mine — one that, were it written with needles at the corners of the eye, would stand as a lesson to whoever took it to heart.
sentences.n: The printed أَوْ ("or") sits exactly where the well-known proverb لَوْ كُتِبَ بِالْإِبَرِ عَلَى آمَاقِ الْبَصَرِ لَكَانَ عِبْرَةً لِمَنِ اعْتَبَرَ ("had it been written with needles at the eye-corners, it would be a lesson to those who take heed") calls for لَوْ ("if, had"). Since لو and أو share no letters, the rasm cannot simply be reread as the proverb; it is kept exactly as printed and vocalized أَوْ, with the almost-certainly-intended sense noted here rather than silently substituted.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ وَكَيْفَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku wa-kayfa dhālika
sentences.l: The king said: And how is that?
sentences.i: The king said: How can that be?

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا سَيِّدِي اعْلَمْ أَنَّ وَالِدِي كَانَ مَلِكَ هَذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā sayyidī iʿlam anna wālidī kāna malika hādhihi al-madīnati
sentences.l: He said: O my lord, know that my father was king of this city.
sentences.i: He said: O my lord, know that my father was king of this city.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ اسْمُهُ مَحْمُودَ صَاحِبَ الْجَزَائِرِ السُّودِ وَهُوَ فِي هَذِهِ الْجِبَالِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna ismuhu Maḥmūdan ṣāḥiba al-jazāʾiri al-sūdi wa-huwa fī hādhihi al-jibāli al-arbaʿati
sentences.l: And his name was Mahmoud, lord of the Black Isles; and he was in these four mountains.
sentences.i: His name was Mahmoud, lord of the Black Islands; and his rule lay among these four mountains.
sentences.n: "Lord of the Black Islands" (صَاحِبُ الْجَزَائِرِ السُّودِ) is a recurring royal title elsewhere in the Nights, attached to a mountain-locked realm rather than islands in the literal sense; the four mountains named here are that realm's landmark.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ فِي الْمُلْكِ سَبْعِينَ عَامًا ثُمَّ تُوُفِّيَ وَالِدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāma fī al-mulki sabʿīna ʿāman thumma tuwuffiya wālidī
sentences.l: And he continued in the kingship seventy years; then my father passed away.
sentences.i: He reigned for seventy years; then my father passed away.

sentences.t: وَ تَسَلْطَنْتُ بَعْدَهُ وَ تَزَوَّجْتُ بِابْنَةِ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: wa-tasalṭantu baʿdahu wa-tazawwajtu bi-ibnati ʿammī
sentences.l: And I became sultan after him, and I married the daughter of my paternal uncle.
sentences.i: I succeeded him as sultan, and I married my cousin, my paternal uncle's daughter.
sentences.n: تَسَلْطَنْتُ is a denominal verb built straight on سُلْطَان ("sultan"), "I made myself/became a sultan" — the kind of verb this narrative Arabic coins freely from titles and nouns.

sentences.t: وَ كَانَتْ تُحِبُّنِي مَحَبَّةً عَظِيمَةً بِحَيْثُ أَنِّي إِذَا غِبْتُ عَنْهَا لَا تَأْكُلُ وَلَا تَشْرَبُ حَتَّى تَرَانِي عِنْدَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kānat tuḥibbunī maḥabbatan ʿaẓīmatan bi-ḥaythu annī idhā ghibtu ʿanhā lā taʾkulu wa-lā tashrabu ḥattā tarānī ʿindahā
sentences.l: And she loved me with a great love, such that I, if I was absent from her, she would not eat and not drink until she saw me with her.
sentences.i: She loved me with an overpowering love — so much so that, if I was ever away from her, she would neither eat nor drink until she saw me at her side.

sentences.t: فَتَعَلَّقَتْ فِي صُحْبَتِي خَمْسَ سِنِينَ إِلَى يَوْمٍ مِنْ بَعْضِ الْأَيَّامِ رَاحَتْ إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿallaqat fī ṣuḥbatī khamsa sinīna ilā yawmin min baʿḍi al-ayyāmi rāḥat ilā al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: And she clung to my company for five years, until a day among the days [when] she went to the bath.
sentences.i: And so she remained bound to my company for five years — until, one day, she went to the baths.

sentences.t: فَأَمَرَتِ الطَّبَّاخَ أَنْ يُسْرِعَ لَنَا فِي شَيْ وَ يُجَهِّزَ لَنَا عَشَاءًا وَ طَعَامًا
sentences.tr: fa-amarati al-ṭabbākha an yusriʿa lanā fī shay wa-yujahhiza lanā ʿashāʾan wa-ṭaʿāman
sentences.l: And she ordered the cook to hasten for us with something, and to prepare for us a dinner and food.
sentences.i: And she ordered the cook to hurry and get something ready for us, and to prepare a dinner and a meal.
sentences.n: شَيْ is printed without its final hamza letter (for شَيْء, "something"); kept exactly as printed and read without a hamza mark, the same treatment this project gives رَدِي for رَدِيء elsewhere in the edition.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَخَلْتُ هَذَا الْقَصْرَ وَ نِمْتُ مَوْضِعَ مَا نَنَامُ
sentences.tr: thumma dakhaltu hādhā al-qaṣra wa-nimtu mawḍiʿa mā nanāmu
sentences.l: Then I entered this castle, and slept in the place where we sleep.
sentences.i: Then I myself went into this castle, and lay down to sleep where we usually slept.
sentences.n: The narration silently shifts from third person (she went, she ordered) to first person here — دَخَلْتُ and نِمْتُ are unambiguously "I," not "she," since the parallel feminine forms would need an extra internal alif (دَخَلَتْ, نَامَتْ) that the rasm does not have.

sentences.t: وَ أَمَرْتُ جَارِيَتَيْنِ أَنْ تَجْلِسَ عِنْدِي وَاحِدَةٌ عَلَى رَأْسِي وَ الثَّانِيَةُ عِنْدَ رِجْلَايَ
sentences.tr: wa-amartu jāriyatayni an tajlisa ʿindī wāḥidatun ʿalā raʾsī wa-al-thāniyatu ʿinda rijlāya
sentences.l: And I ordered two slave-girls that one sit with me at my head, and the other at my feet.
sentences.i: And I ordered two slave-girls to sit with me — one at my head, and the other at my feet.
sentences.n: After عِنْدَ one expects the oblique dual رِجْلَيَّ; the edition instead spells it with the nominative-looking ending (رجلاي, rijlāya), a case-leveling typical of this text's Middle Arabic, kept as printed here and again at the very end of this excerpt.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ تَشَوَّشْتُ لِغِيَابِهَا وَلَمْ يَأْخُذْنِي نَوْمٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qad tashawwashtu li-ghiyābihā wa-lam yaʾkhudhnī nawmun
sentences.l: And I was troubled by her absence, and sleep did not take me.
sentences.i: I grew uneasy at her absence, and sleep would not come to me.

sentences.t: غَيْرَ أَنَّ عَيْنِي مُغْمَضَةٌ وَ نَفْسِي يَقْظَانَةٌ
sentences.tr: ghayra anna ʿaynī mughmaḍatun wa-nafsī yaqẓānatun
sentences.l: Except that my eye was closed, and my soul was wakeful.
sentences.i: Only my eyes were shut, while my mind stayed fully awake.

sentences.t: فَسَمِعْتُ الْجَارِيَةَ الَّتِي عِنْدَ رَأْسِي تَقُولُ لِلَّتِي عِنْدَ رِجْلَايَ
sentences.tr: fa-samiʿtu al-jāriyata allatī ʿinda raʾsī taqūlu li-allatī ʿinda rijlāya
sentences.l: And I heard the slave-girl who was at my head saying to the one who was at my feet —
sentences.i: Then I heard the slave-girl at my head say to the one at my feet —
sentences.n: The excerpt breaks off here, on the threshold of the gossip the two slave-girls are about to exchange.

sentences.t: يَا مَسْعُودَةُ مِسْكِينٌ سَيِّدُنَا وَ مِسْكِينٌ شَبَابُهُ وَ يَا خَسَارَتَهُ مَعَ سِتِّنَا الْمَلْعُونَةِ الْقَحْبَةِ
sentences.tr: yā Masʿūdatu miskīnun sayyidunā wa-miskīnun shabābuhu wa-yā khasāratahu maʿa sittinā al-malʿūnati al-qaḥbati
sentences.l: O Masʿūda, poor is our master, and poor is his youth, and O his waste, with our cursed mistress, the whore!
sentences.i: O Masʿūda, how I pity our master, and pity his youth — what a waste of him, tied to our cursed mistress, the whore!
sentences.n: سِتّ ('sitt', here in 'sittinā', 'our mistress') is the colloquial word for 'lady, mistress', distinct from Classical sayyida; kept as the edition's own usage. Here the archive prints وَ twice as its own space-delimited word rather than fused onto the next ('سيدنا و مسكين ... شبابه و يا'), unlike its usual fused spelling elsewhere in this slice; both spellings are kept exactly as printed. This sentence continues without a break the speech begun in the preceding slice, spoken by the slave-girl the narrator — the enchanted prince, telling his own story in the first person — describes as posted at his own head.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا نَعَمْ لَعَنَ اللَّهُ النِّسَاءَ الْخَائِنَاتِ الزَّانِيَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā naʿam laʿana Allāhu al-nisāʾa al-khāʾināti al-zāniyāti
sentences.l: So she said to her: Yes — may God curse treacherous, adulterous women.
sentences.i: So she answered her: Yes — God curse unfaithful, adulterous women!

sentences.t: وَلَٰكِنْ مِثْلُ سَيِّدِنَا وَشَبَابِهِ لَا يَصْلُحُ لِهَٰذِهِ الْقَحْبَةِ كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ تَنَامُ بَرًّا
sentences.tr: wa-lākin mithlu sayyidinā wa-shabābihi lā yaṣluḥu li-hādhihi al-qaḥbati kulla laylatin tanāmu barran
sentences.l: But the like of our master, and his youth — it is not fitting for this whore: every night she sleeps outside.
sentences.i: But a man like our master, and his youth besides, deserve better than this whore, who sleeps abroad every single night.
sentences.n: كل ليلة تنام برا is an asyndetic relative clause with no relative pronoun — '[who] sleeps outside every night' — a normal feature of this narrative Arabic.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الَّتِي عِنْدَ رَأْسِي سَيِّدُنَا أَبْكَمُ مَطْعُومٌ أَمْ يَسْأَلُ عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālati allatī ʿinda raʾsī sayyidunā abkamu maṭʿūmun am yasʾalu ʿanhā
sentences.l: So she said, the one who was at my head: Is our master dumb, fed, or does he ask about her?
sentences.i: Then the one at my head said: Is our master simply dumb and complacent, or does he ever ask after her?
sentences.n: التي عند رأسي, 'the one at my head', is the narrator's own first-person framing — the enchanted prince recalls that one slave-girl was posted at his own head and the other at his feet as he lay feigning sleep. أَبْكَمُ مَطْعُومٌ, 'dumb, well-fed', reads as a set description of someone too complacent or oblivious to notice what is under his own nose.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْأُخْرَى وَيْلَكِ هُوَ سَيِّدُنَا عِنْدَهُ عِلْمٌ أَوْ هِيَ تُخَلِّيهِ فِي اخْتِيَارِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ukhrā waylaki huwa sayyidunā ʿindahu ʿilmun aw hiya tukhallīhi fī ikhtiyārihi
sentences.l: So the other said: Woe to you! Is it that our master has knowledge (of it), or is it that she leaves him to his own choosing?
sentences.i: The other replied: Curse you — does our master know anything of this, or does she simply let him do as he pleases?

sentences.t: أَلَا تَعْمَلُ لَهُ فِي قَدَحِ الشَّرَابِ الَّذِي تَشْرَبُهُ كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ قَبْلَ الْمَنَامِ وَتَضَعُ فِيهِ الْبَنْجَ
sentences.tr: alā taʿmalu lahu fī qadaḥi al-sharābi alladhī tashrabuhu kulla laylatin qabla al-manāmi wa-taḍaʿu fīhi al-banja
sentences.l: Does she not work upon him, in the cup of the drink that he drinks every night before sleep — and put into it the banj?
sentences.i: Does she not drug him — putting the banj into the cup of the drink he takes every night before bed?
sentences.n: بَنْج (banj) is a sedative or knock-out drug, a recurring device in the Nights; it is glossed here at its first appearance in this tale and will recur. The verb تَشْرَبُهُ ('she/you drink it') is marked for a feminine or second-person subject rather than the masculine 'he drinks it' (يشربه) the sense requires — one more instance of this text's loose subject concord — and is translated here by evident sense.

sentences.t: فَيَنَامُ وَلَمْ يَشْعُرْ بِمَا يَجْرِي وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَيْنَ يَذْهَبُ وَلَا أَيْنَ تَرُوحُ
sentences.tr: fa-yanāmu wa-lam yashʿur bimā yajrī wa-lam yaʿlam ayna yadhhabu wa-lā ayna tarūḥu
sentences.l: So he sleeps, and does not perceive what happens, and does not know where he goes, nor where she goes.
sentences.i: So he falls asleep, knowing nothing of what happens — not where she goes, nor where she goes off to.
sentences.n: The first verb of place, يَذْهَبُ, is masculine ('where he goes'), while the second, تَرُوحُ, is feminine ('where she goes') — both evidently meant of the wife's own coming and going, despite the gender switch; ذهب and راح form a common near-synonym doublet in this prose.

sentences.t: فَبَعْدَ مَا تَسْقِيهِ الشَّرَابَ تَلْبَسُ أَثْوَابَهَا وَتَعَطَّرَتْ وَتَخْرُجُ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-baʿda mā tasqīhi al-sharāba talbasu athwābahā wa-taʿaṭṭarat wa-takhruju min ʿindihi
sentences.l: Then after she gives him the drink to drink, she puts on her garments, and she perfumed herself, and she goes out from him.
sentences.i: Then, once she has given him the drink, she dresses, perfumes herself, and slips out from beside him.
sentences.n: The tense shifts from imperfect (talbasu, takhruju) to a bare perfect (taʿaṭṭarat, 'she perfumed herself') in the middle of this string of habitual actions — a feature of this text's narration, kept as printed rather than regularized.

sentences.t: تَغِيبُ إِلَى الْفَجْرِ وَتَأْتِي إِلَيْهِ وَتُبَخِّرُ عِنْدَهُ أَنْفَهُ بِشَيٍّ
sentences.tr: taghību ilā al-fajri wa-taʾtī ilayhi wa-tubakhkhiru ʿindahu anfahu bi-shayyin
sentences.l: She stays away until the dawn, and comes to him, and fumigates near him — his nose — with something…
sentences.i: She stays away until nearly dawn, then comes back to him and holds something smoking under his nose…
sentences.n: The archive's line breaks off here, at بشي, printed without the final hamza-letter of شيء ('something'); by analogy with this text's similar smoothing of hamza-final roots elsewhere (compare ردي for رديء in Night 6), it is read here as بِشَيٍّ, the missing hamza absorbed into a doubled final yāʾ. The clause is left incomplete — presumably naming what she burns to rouse him — because the given slice ends exactly at this word.

sentences.t: فَيَسْتَيْقِظُ مِنْ مَنَامِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-yastayqiẓu min manāmihi
sentences.l: So he wakes up from his sleep.
sentences.n: This short clause closes the slave-girls' report from the preceding passage — a habitual, generic imperfect describing what happens every night, per the gossip just overheard — before the narration turns to the prince's own reaction.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ كَلَامَ الْجَوَارِي صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي وَجْهِي ظَلَامَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu kalāma al-jawārī ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhī ẓalāmahu
sentences.l: And when I heard the words of the slave-girls, the light in my face became its darkness.
sentences.i: When I heard what the slave-girls said, the very light before my eyes turned to darkness.
sentences.n: The idiom echoes the frame story's set phrase for despair, 'the world blackened in his face' (iswaddat al-dunyā fī wajhihi) — the same grief located 'in the face,' phrased here as light turning into its own darkness.

sentences.t: وَمَا صَدَّقْتُ أَنَّ اللَّيْلَ أَقْبَلَ فَجَاءَتْ بِنْتُ عَمِّي مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā ṣaddaqtu anna al-layla aqbala fa-jāʾat bintu ʿammī mina al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: And I did not believe that the night had come — then my cousin came from the bath.
sentences.i: I could scarcely believe that night had come at last, when my cousin arrived home from the baths.
sentences.n: 'بنت عمي,' 'my (paternal) cousin,' is how the prince refers throughout to his wife, his father's brother's daughter.

sentences.t: فَمَدَدْنَا السِّمَاطَ وَأَكَلْنَا وَجَلَسْنَا سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً نَتَنَادَمُ كَالْعَادَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-madadnā al-simāṭa wa-akalnā wa-jalasnā sāʿatan zamāniyyatan natanādamu ka-al-ʿādati
sentences.l: So we spread the table-cloth and ate, and sat a good while, conversing together as usual.
sentences.i: So we spread the cloth and ate, and sat together a good while, keeping each other company as was our habit.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَعَتْ بِالشَّرَابِ الَّذِي أَشْرَبُهُ عِنْدَ الْمَنَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma daʿat bi-al-sharābi alladhī ashrabuhu ʿinda al-manāmi
sentences.l: Then she called for the drink that I drink at bedtime.

sentences.t: فَنَاوَلَتْنِي الْكَأْسَ فَهَرَقْتُهَا وَجَعَلْتُ أَنِّي أَشْرَبُهُ مِثْلَ عَادَتِي وَدَلَقْتُهُ فِي جَيْبِي وَرَقَدْتُ فِي الْوَقْتِ وَ السَّاعَةِ وَصِرْتُ أَخْطُرُ كَأَنِّي نَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: fa-nāwalatnī al-kaʾsa fa-haraqtuhā wa-jaʿaltu annī ashrabuhu mithla ʿādatī wa-dalaqtuhu fī jaybī wa-raqadtu fī al-waqti wa-al-sāʿati wa-ṣirtu akhṭuru ka-annī nāʾimun
sentences.l: So she handed me the cup; I poured it away, and made as though I drank it, as was my custom, and tipped it into my bosom, and lay down on the instant, and I began to stir as though I were asleep.
sentences.i: She handed me the cup. I poured it out and made a show of drinking it down as I always did, tipping it instead into the fold of my robe, and lay down then and there, feigning the movements of a sleeper.
sentences.n: أَخْطُرُ is unusual here: khaṭara ordinarily means 'to occur to the mind' or 'to swagger, sway'; its sense while lying down and feigning sleep is uncertain — perhaps 'to stir, toss' or 'to breathe heavily' — and it is vocalized here by best guess rather than emended. The pouring-away is also given twice in near-duplicate (haraqtuhā ... dalaqtuhu fī jaybī), perhaps an emphatic doubling rather than two distinct acts.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا هِيَ قَالَتْ نَمْ لَيْلَتَكَ لَا تَقُمْ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: wa-idhā hiya qālat nam laylataka lā taqum abadan
sentences.l: And behold, she said: 'Sleep your night away — never get up again!'
sentences.i: And there she was, saying: 'Sleep on through the night — and never wake again!'

sentences.t: وَاللَّهِ كَرِهْتُكَ وَكَرِهْتُ صُورَتَكَ وَمَلَّتْ نَفْسِي مِنْ عِشْرَتِكَ وَلَا أَدْرِي مَتَى يَقْبِضُ اللَّهُ رُوحَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi karihtuka wa-karihtu ṣūrataka wa-mallat nafsī min ʿishratika wa-lā adrī matā yaqbiḍu Allāhu rūḥaka
sentences.l: By God, I hate you, and I hate your form, and my soul is weary of your company, and I do not know when God will seize your soul.
sentences.i: By God, I hate you, I hate the very sight of you, and I am sick to my soul of your company — and I do not know when God will take your life.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ وَلَبِسَتْ أَفْخَرَ ثِيَابِهَا وَ تَبَخَّرَتْ وَأَخَذَتْ سَيْفِي وَتَقَلَّدَتْ بِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat wa-labisat afkhara thiyābihā wa-tabakhkharat wa-akhadhat sayfī wa-taqalladat bihi
sentences.l: Then she rose, and put on her finest clothes, and perfumed herself with incense, and took my sword, and girded herself with it.
sentences.i: Then she got up, dressed in her finest clothes, perfumed herself, took my own sword, and buckled it on.

sentences.t: وَفَتَحَتْ أَبْوَابَ الْقَصْرِ وَخَرَجَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-fataḥat abwāba al-qaṣri wa-kharajat
sentences.l: And she opened the doors of the castle and went out.

sentences.t: فَقُمْتُ وَتَبِعْتُهَا حَتَّى خَرَجَتْ مِنَ الْقَصْرِ وَشَقَّتْ فِي أَسْوَاقِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qumtu wa-tabiʿtuhā ḥattā kharajat mina al-qaṣri wa-shaqqat fī aswāqi al-madīnati
sentences.l: So I got up and followed her, until she left the castle and cut through the markets of the city.
sentences.i: So I rose and followed her, until she had left the castle and was making her way through the city's markets.

sentences.t: إِلَى أَنِ انْتَهَتْ إِلَى بَابِ الْمَدِينَهْ فَتَكَلَّمَتْ بِكَلَامٍ لَا أَفْهَمُهُ فَتَسَاقَطَتِ الْأَقْفَالُ وَانْفَتَحَ الْبَابُ
sentences.tr: ilā ani intahat ilā bābi al-madīnah fa-takallamat bi-kalāmin lā afhamuhu fa-tasāqaṭati al-aqfālu wa-infataḥa al-bābu
sentences.l: until she reached the gate of the city; then she spoke words I did not understand, and the locks fell away one after another, and the gate opened.
sentences.i: until she reached the city gate. There she spoke words I could not understand, and the locks dropped away of themselves, and the gate swung open.
sentences.n: المدينه is here spelled with plain hāʾ rather than the tāʾ marbūṭa used for the same word one sentence earlier (aswāqi al-madīnati) — a Middle Arabic scribal inconsistency kept exactly as printed; it is still read al-madīnah.

sentences.t: وَخَرَجَتْ وَأَنَا خَلْفَهَا وَهِيَ لَا تَشْعُرُ حَتَّى انْتَهَتْ إِلَى بَيْنِ الْكِيمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-kharajat wa-anā khalfahā wa-hiya lā tashʿuru ḥattā intahat ilā bayni al-kīmāni
sentences.l: And she went out, with me behind her, she not perceiving, until she came to among the mounds.
sentences.i: And she went out, with me behind her all unknown to her, until she came to a place among the rubble-mounds.

sentences.t: وَأَتَتْ إِلَى خُصٍّ فِيهِ قُبَّةٌ مَبْنِيَّةٌ بِطُوبٍ وَلَهَا بَابٌ
sentences.tr: wa-atat ilā khuṣṣin fīhi qubbatun mabniyyatun bi-ṭūbin wa-lahā bābun
sentences.l: And she came to a hut in which was a dome built of brick, having a door.
sentences.i: And she came to a reed hut, inside which stood a dome built of brick, with a door of its own.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَتْ وَتَسَلَّقْتُ أَنَا عَلَى سَطْحِ الْقُبَّةِ وَأَشْرَفْتُ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalat wa-tasallaqtu anā ʿalā saṭḥi al-qubbati wa-ashraftu ʿalayhim
sentences.l: So she went in, and I climbed up onto the roof of the dome, and I looked down upon them.
sentences.i: She went inside, and I climbed onto the roof of the dome and looked down over them.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِبِنْتِ عَمِّي قَدْ دَخَلَتْ عَلَى عَبْدٍ أَسْوَدَ لَهُ شَفَةٌ كَالْقَطَا وَشَفَةٌ كَالْوَطَا وَشَفَةٌ تَلْقُطُ الرَّمْلَ عَلَى الْحَصَا
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-binti ʿammī qad dakhalat ʿalā ʿabdin aswada lahu shafatun ka-al-qaṭā wa-shafatun ka-al-waṭā wa-shafatun talquṭu al-ramla ʿalā al-ḥaṣā
sentences.l: And behold, my cousin had gone in to a black slave, who had a lip like the sand-grouse, and a lip like the trodden ground, and a lip that gathers the sand from among the pebbles.
sentences.i: And there was my cousin — she had gone in to a black slave, a creature with a lip like a sand-grouse, a lip like the bare trodden ground, a lip that swept the sand up from among the pebbles.
sentences.n: This clause and the two that follow it form a small chain of sajʿ rhyming on -ā (qaṭā / waṭā / ḥaṣā). The threefold repetition of shafatun, 'a lip,' is most likely a rhetorical device intensifying one grotesque image (the slave's huge, hanging lip) rather than a literal count of lips, and is left exactly as printed; the description continues in the clause that follows. The precise point of comparison to qaṭā (the sand-grouse) and waṭā ('trodden, low ground') is not certain — stock hyperbole of the kind used elsewhere in the Nights for black slaves.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ مُبْتَلًى وَرَاقِدٌ عَلَى قَشِّ قَصَبٍ لَابِسٌ هِدْمَةً وَشَرَامِيطَ خَلِقَةً
sentences.tr: wa-huwa mubtalan wa-rāqidun ʿalā qashshi qaṣabin lābisun hidmatan wa-sharāmīṭa khaliqatan
sentences.l: and he was afflicted, and lying on the chaff of cane, wearing a worn-out garment and tattered old rags.
sentences.i: He lay there afflicted, stretched out on a litter of reed-chaff, dressed in a ragged garment and worn old tatters.
sentences.n: مُبْتَلًى, 'afflicted,' leaves the nature of the affliction unstated — perhaps disease — in keeping with the squalor of the straw bedding and rags.

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلَتِ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbalati al-arḍa bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: Then she kissed the ground before him.

sentences.t: فَشَالَ ذَلِكَ الْعَبْدُ رَأْسَهُ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-shāla dhālika al-ʿabdu raʾsahu ilayhā
sentences.l: Then that slave raised his head toward her.
sentences.n: شَالَ is the colloquial equivalent of رَفَعَ, 'to lift, raise,' common in this narrative register.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهَا وَيْلَكِي أَيْشْ كَانَ قُعَادُكِ إِلَى هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahā waylakī aysh kāna quʿāduki ilā hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: And he said to her: 'Woe to you! What was your sitting until this hour?'
sentences.i: And he said to her: 'Damn you! What kept you sitting away until this hour?'
sentences.n: أَيْش is the colloquial contraction of أَيُّ شَيْءٍ, 'what (thing)'; قُعَادُكِ, 'your sitting, tarrying,' is a colloquial verbal noun from قَعَدَ.

sentences.t: كَانُوا عِنْدَنَا بَنُوا أَعْمَامِنَا السُّودَانُ وَشَرِبُوا الشَّرَابَ وَصَارَ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ بِصَبِيَّتِهِ وَأَنَا مَا رَضِيتُ أَشْرَبَ مِنْ شَأْنِكِ
sentences.tr: kānū ʿindanā banū aʿmāminā al-sūdānu wa-sharibū al-sharāba wa-ṣāra kullu wāḥidin bi-ṣabiyyatihi wa-anā mā raḍītu ashraba min shaʾnik
sentences.l: They were with us — our paternal-uncles'-sons, the blacks — and they drank the wine, and each one became with his girl; but I — I did not consent [to] drink, from your affair.
sentences.i: 'Our fellow blacks were there with us, and they drank their wine and each of them paired off with his girl — but I would not drink, on your account.'
sentences.n: بنو اعمامنا السودان, literally 'the sons of our paternal uncles, the blacks', is a kinship idiom of solidarity among the slaves — 'our own black brethren' — not a claim of literal cousinhood. من شانك, 'from your affair', is the idiom for 'for your sake, on your account'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يَا سَيِّدِي وَحَبِيبِي وَ قُرَّةَ عَيْنِي مَا تَعْلَمُ أَنِّي مُتَزَوِّجَةٌ بِابْنِ عَمِّي وَأَنَا أَكْرَهُ صُورَتَهُ وَأَبْغُضُ صُحْبَتَهُ
